name: LLM & Generative-AI Security
description: Security and privacy of large language models and generative AI: prompt injection, jailbreaks, and LLM-assisted security.

uss.narrative:
USENIX Security's engagement with LLM and AI security began before large generative models dominated headlines. Early work focused on NLP-backed threat intelligence: Reading Thieves' Cant (USENIX 2018) showed automated NLP could interpret obfuscated criminal jargon on dark-web markets. As DNN-based text classifiers became deployment targets, T-Miner (USENIX 2021) proposed a generative defence against Trojan triggers embedded in those classifiers — one of the first USENIX papers treating an NLP model itself as an adversarial target. Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack on NLP Models via Linguistic Style Manipulation (USENIX 2022) then showed the attack side: linguistic style alone could serve as a stealthy backdoor trigger, raising the threat bar for any organization deploying fine-tuned language models.

The arrival of large generative models in 2023 produced an immediate wave of privacy and integrity research. Glaze (USENIX 2023) tackled a new harm — artists' visual style being mimicked by text-to-image models — and proposed perturbation-based protection that sparked significant real-world adoption. CodexLeaks (USENIX 2023) demonstrated that code-generation models like GitHub Copilot memorize and regurgitate private training data, establishing a template for LLM memorisation audits. Two-in-One (USENIX 2023) introduced the concept of model hijacking, repurposing a deployed text-generation model for an attacker's covert task, extending prior classification-model attack ideas to the generative setting.

By 2024, safety alignment and jailbreaking became the dominant research front. Making Them Ask and Answer (USENIX 2024) broke alignment in a small number of queries via a disguise-and-reconstruct technique; LLM-Fuzzer (USENIX 2024) turned classic fuzzing methodology into a scalable jailbreak template generator, demonstrating that safety evaluation is fundamentally a fuzzing problem. Instruction Backdoor Attacks Against Customized LLMs (USENIX 2024) moved beyond public models to attack the GPT-style customization layer, while Malla (USENIX 2024) measured the real underground economy of LLM-integrated criminal services. The What Was Your Prompt? attack (USENIX 2024) exposed a side-channel in encrypted AI-assistant traffic that could reconstruct users' queries from token-length patterns alone.

The 2025 cohort reflects maturation on both attack and defence fronts. JBShield (USENIX 2025) countered jailbreaks by analysing activated internal concepts to detect and neutralise disguised inputs at inference time. Research expanded into agent-level threats: Make Agent Defeat Agent (USENIX 2025) used one LLM agent to automatically surface taint-style vulnerabilities in another, and Cloak, Honey, Trap (USENIX 2025) developed proactive honeypot defences against autonomous LLM penetration-testing agents. RAG-specific attack vectors also emerged — PoisonedRAG and Topic-FlipRAG (USENIX 2025) showed that injecting crafted documents into a retrieval corpus could hijack or manipulate grounded LLM outputs, opening a new poisoning surface as RAG deployment spread.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this list predates the large-language-model era and framed the problem as one of adversarial robustness for text classifiers. TextBugger: Generating Adversarial Text Against Real-world Applications (NDSS 2019) showed that small, human-imperceptible perturbations could flip the decisions of deployed sentiment- and toxicity-detection systems, establishing that natural-language models were attackable in the same spirit as image classifiers. A few years later, Interpretable Federated Transformer Log Learning for Cloud Threat Forensics (NDSS 2022) marked a pivot in the other direction — using transformer models as defensive tooling for threat detection and forensics — foreshadowing the "LLM-assisted security" thread that now runs through the whole area.

By 2024 the field reorganized around generative LLMs themselves, splitting into offense and defense. On the offense side, MASTERKEY: Automated Jailbreaking of Large Language Model Chatbots (NDSS 2024) automated the discovery of prompts that bypass safety guardrails, while a cluster of defensive papers hardened models against poisoning and backdoors — TextGuard: Provable Defense against Backdoor Attacks on Text Classification, LMSanitator: Defending Prompt-Tuning Against Task-Agnostic Backdoors, and Improving the Robustness of Transformer-based Large Language Models with Dynamic Attention (all NDSS 2024). In parallel, LLMs became security instruments: Large Language Model guided Protocol Fuzzing and DeGPT: Optimizing Decompiler Output with LLM (both NDSS 2024) showed that models could drive fuzzing and reverse engineering, turning generative AI into a productivity multiplier for vulnerability discovery.

NDSS 2025 broadened the attack surface from the model to the serving system and the deployment pipeline. I Know What You Asked: Prompt Leakage via KV-Cache Sharing in Multi-Tenant LLM Serving (NDSS 2025) exposed a systems-level side channel that leaks user prompts across tenants, while Safety Misalignment Against Large Language Models (NDSS 2025) studied how cheaply alignment can be undone. The LLM-as-tool line matured with evaluations and pipelines such as From Large to Mammoth: A Comparative Evaluation of Large Language Models in Vulnerability Detection, YuraScanner: Leveraging LLMs for Task-driven Web App Scanning, and PropertyGPT: LLM-driven Formal Verification of Smart Contracts (all NDSS 2025), and privacy/abuse concerns extended to generative media with THEMIS: Regulating Textual Inversion for Personalized Concept Censorship and Towards Understanding Unsafe Video Generation.

The most recent work (NDSS 2026) reflects a maturing, systems-and-ecosystem view. Infrastructure attacks deepen with Cache Me, Catch You: Cache Related Security Threats in LLM Serving Frameworks and When Cache Poisoning Meets LLM Systems: Semantic Cache Poisoning and Its Countermeasures, while new subtleties emerge in Trust Me, I Know This Function: Hijacking LLM Static Analysis using Bias, which shows attackers can manipulate the very LLM-based analyzers the 2024 papers introduced. The agenda now spans agentic tooling (FirmAgent: Leveraging Fuzzing to Assist LLM Agents with IoT Firmware Vulnerability Discovery), governance and content moderation (Characterizing the Implementation of Censorship Policies in Chinese LLM Services; There is No War in Ba Sing Se: A Global Analysis of Content Moderation in Large Language Models), and privacy-preserving deployment (Prεεmpt: Sanitizing Sensitive Prompts for LLMs). Tellingly, the field has also turned reflective: Chasing Shadows: Pitfalls in LLM Security Research (NDSS 2026) catalogs methodological mistakes, a sign that LLM security has matured enough to critique its own evaluation practices.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this area treated language models mainly as a new privacy surface rather than an adversarial target. "Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models" (S&P 2020) kicked things off by showing that embeddings from BERT/GPT-style models leak sensitive attributes of their inputs, and the following year the concern broadened to provenance and misuse: "Adversarial Watermarking Transformer" (S&P 2021) hid traceable signals in generated text, while "Self-Supervised Euphemism Detection and Identification for Content Moderation" (S&P 2021) turned generation models toward the defensive problem of spotting coded abusive language. The through-line was a research community still thinking in classic ML-security terms.

That framing sharpened in 2022 with concrete attack primitives. "Bad Characters: Imperceptible NLP Attacks" (S&P 2022) showed invisible Unicode perturbations could break text pipelines, and two backdoor papers — "Piccolo: Exposing Complex Backdoors in NLP Transformer Models" and "Spinning Language Models: Risks of Propaganda-As-A-Service" (both S&P 2022) — established training-time poisoning as a first-class threat. By 2023 the field had split into memorization and code-security tracks: "Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models" (S&P 2023) made PII extraction rigorous, while "Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models" (S&P 2023) and "Deepfake Text Detection" (S&P 2023) opened the twin questions of using LLMs for defense and detecting their output.

The 2024–2025 wave is where prompt injection, jailbreaks, and generative-model abuse became the center of gravity. "SneakyPrompt: Jailbreaking Text-to-image Generative Models" (S&P 2024) and "Nightshade: Prompt-Specific Poisoning Attacks" (S&P 2024) attacked diffusion models directly, while sober evaluations like "LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities (Yet?)" (S&P 2024) tempered the hype around LLM-assisted security, and "From Chatbots to Phishbots?" (S&P 2024) documented real offensive misuse. Poisoned-code work ("TrojanPuzzle," "Poisoned ChatGPT Finds Work for Idle Hands," both S&P 2024) targeted the coding-assistant supply chain. By 2025 defenses matured: "DataSentinel: A Game-Theoretic Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks" (S&P 2025) and the systematizing "SoK: Watermarking for AI-Generated Content" (S&P 2025) show the community trying to consolidate, even as "UnMarker: A Universal Attack on Defensive Image Watermarking" (S&P 2025) proved those defenses remain fragile.

The most recent 2026 papers signal a move toward deployed, multi-modal, and agentic systems. Attacks now hit new surfaces — "Hijacking Large Audio-Language Models via Context-Agnostic and Imperceptible Auditory Prompt Injection" and "Investigating the Impact of Dark Patterns on LLM-Based Web Agents" (both S&P 2026) — while the app-store ecosystem gets probed by "LLMThief: Evaluating Configuration Leaking Risks in Commercial LLM App Stores" (S&P 2026). Defense has become more surgical, with "PromptLocate: Localizing Prompt Injection Attacks" (S&P 2026) moving from detection to pinpointing the injected span, and infrastructure-level concerns appear in "Euston: Efficient and User-Friendly Secure Transformer Inference" and "Hollow-LLM Attack" on zero-knowledge verification of LLM inference (both S&P 2026). The area has grown from a privacy footnote about embeddings into a full sub-discipline spanning attacks, defenses, agents, and verifiable serving.

ccs.narrative:
LLM and generative AI security emerged as a major CCS research area almost simultaneously with the public release of large foundation models. The 2023 cohort established the initial threat landscape across three domains. Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (CCS 2023) quantified the real-world risk of AI code generation. DE-FAKE: Detection and Attribution of Fake Images Generated by Text-to-Image Generation Models (CCS 2023) addressed synthetic media forensics. Unsafe Diffusion: On the Generation of Unsafe Images and Hateful Memes From Text-To-Image Models (CCS 2023) measured how diffusion models can be prompted to produce harmful content.

By 2024, jailbreaks and prompt injection became primary attack categories. "Do Anything Now": Characterizing and Evaluating In-The-Wild Jailbreak Prompts on Large Language Models (CCS 2024) systematically categorized jailbreak prompts collected from the wild, measuring their effectiveness across models. Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge (CCS 2024) showed that LLM-as-judge evaluation pipelines are manipulable via adversarial inputs. PLeak: Prompt Leaking Attacks against Large Language Model Applications (CCS 2024) demonstrated extraction of confidential system prompts.

Backdoor attacks against pre-trained models had been anticipated: Backdoor Pre-trained Models Can Transfer to All (CCS 2021) showed that trojan backdoors survive fine-tuning in NLP, foreshadowing the LLM supply-chain threat. zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models (CCS 2024) closed the loop by enabling verifiable inference, providing a cryptographic foundation for trustworthy LLM deployment.

milestones.title: Backdoor Pre-trained Models Can Transfer to All
milestones.note: Showed backdoors in pre-trained NLP models persist across any downstream fine-tuning, warning of LLM supply-chain risks.

milestones.note: Produced the first ZK proofs for correct LLM inference at scale, enabling trustworthy verifiable AI deployment.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection treats language models less as conversational agents and more as opaque statistical systems whose text outputs could betray secrets or be nudged into mistakes. "Reading Thieves' Cant" (USENIX 2018) used generative language modeling defensively, to decode obfuscated cybercrime jargon, while "TextBugger" (NDSS 2019) showed that small, often imperceptible perturbations could fool real-world text classifiers. By "Privacy Risks of General-Purpose Language Models" (S&P 2020), the field had squarely identified that BERT- and GPT-style embeddings leak sensitive attributes of their inputs, framing pretrained models themselves as an attack surface.

The early 2020s were dominated by supply-chain and integrity threats. A cluster of backdoor and Trojan papers — "Backdoor Pre-trained Models Can Transfer to All" (CCS 2021), "Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack on NLP Models" (USENIX 2022), and the "Piccolo" defense (S&P 2022) — worried about poisoned models and hidden triggers, while "Bad Characters: Imperceptible NLP Attacks" (S&P 2022) and "Spinning Language Models" (S&P 2022) extended adversarial and propaganda risks. In parallel, privacy sharpened into concrete extraction, with "Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models" (S&P 2023) quantifying how models regurgitate PII. Two other 2023 shifts mattered: generative image models arrived as a threat surface — "Glaze" (USENIX 2023), "DE-FAKE" and "Unsafe Diffusion" (CCS 2023) — and researchers began asking whether LLMs help or hurt security work, with "Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?" (CCS 2023) and "Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair" (S&P 2023) giving sobering, mixed answers.

By 2024 the modern agenda crystallized around deployed chat models and the prompt as the attack vector. "'Do Anything Now'" (CCS 2024) systematized in-the-wild jailbreaks, "LLM-Fuzzer" (USENIX 2024) scaled jailbreak discovery, and prompt-level attacks matured through "Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge," "PLeak" prompt-leaking, and "Instruction Backdoor Attacks Against Customized LLMs" (all CCS/USENIX 2024). The same models were also turned into tools — "PentestGPT" (USENIX 2024), "Large Language Model guided Protocol Fuzzing" and "DeGPT" decompilation (NDSS 2024) — even as "LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities (Yet?)" (S&P 2024) cautioned against overtrust. Text-to-image attacks continued with "SneakyPrompt" and "Nightshade" (S&P 2024). Defenses began to answer back in 2025 via "SecAlign" (CCS 2025) and "DataSentinel" (S&P 2025).

The most recent work, concentrated in NDSS 2026, shows a field turning both broader and more self-critical. Applications keep widening — LLM-driven PLC fuzzing, TEE-boundary code annotation, hallucination-reduced incident-response planning, and human-LLM teaming in reverse engineering — while new failure modes surface, such as "Trust Me, I Know This Function: Hijacking LLM Static Analysis using Bias." Privacy and governance concerns mature into prompt sanitization ("Prεεmpt") and studies of state censorship in "Chinese LLM Services." Tellingly, "Chasing Shadows: Pitfalls in LLM Security Research" (NDSS 2026) steps back to critique the methodology of the field itself — a sign that LLM and generative-AI security has grown from scattered attacks into a discipline now auditing its own rigor.
